messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.

I'm after roughly 1,600 ft of altitude. Total impulse has to stay under 160 Ns. It should land under 18 ft/s. The rail is 6 ft long. The launch site is at 2,500 ft elevation. Provide the design and expected performance.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: apogee about 1,600 ft = 1600 * 0.3048 = 488 m (approximate, aim within 5%). Total impulse under 160 N*s (maximum). Touchdown under 18 ft/s = 18 * 0.3048 = 5.5 m/s (maximum). Rail is 6 ft = 6 * 0.3048 = 1.83 m (fixed). Site elevation 2,500 ft = 2500 * 0.3048 = 762 m (fixed). Wind is not stated, so I assume 2 m/s. One stage.
2. Feasibility: 160 N*s caps this at an F or a small G. Ballistic speed for 488 m is sqrt(2*9.81*488) = 97.8 m/s before drag, so a mid-power airframe probably wants 70 to 110 N*s installed to hit the window without blowing past it. The candidate band is a light F, a strong F and a modest G; checking F15, F32T and G64W.

2. Feasibility: the F15 at 49.6 N*s leaves little drag margin for 488 m and its 14.5 N average thrust gives a slow rail exit. The G64W at 118 N*s fits under the 160 N*s cap but on a light airframe it would sail well past the window. The F32T at 56.7 N*s and 34.2 N average is the middle option and the first choice.
3. Size: airframe about 0.18 kg plus the 0.064 kg motor gives liftoff near 0.25 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 34.2 / (0.25 * 9.81) = 13.9, well above 3. Rail exit on the 1.83 m rail: a = (34.2 - 2.45) / 0.25 = 127 m/s^2, so v = sqrt(2 * 127 * 1.83) = 21.6 m/s. Ideal delta-v = 56.7 / 0.25 = 227 m/s; the ballistic ceiling from that is far past 488 m, so whether this lands in the window comes down to drag on a 41.6 mm body at altitude. Descent mass is about 0.25 - 0.026 = 0.22 kg. At 762 m elevation the air density is roughly 1.1 kg/m^3, and a 0.55 m chute (area 0.238 m^2) at Cd 0.8 gives v = sqrt(2 * 0.22 * 9.81 / (1.1 * 0.8 * 0.238)) = 4.5 m/s, under the 5.5 m/s limit. Apogee should come near 7 to 9 s, so the 6 s delay is the first guess.
4. Draft: 41.6 mm card body, 0.55 m long, solid balsa ogive nose, three birch-ply fins, 25.5 mm mount for the 24 mm F32T-6, 0.55 m ripstop chute on motor ejection. Simulating at the stated 1.83 m rail and 762 m site elevation.

4. Check: the simulated apogee of 676.8 m sits 39% above the 488 m goal, far outside the 5% band, so the altitude target fails on this draft. Every safety gate passes: rail exit 33.0 m/s, thrust-to-weight 19.0, margin 1.54 cal at rail exit, touchdown 4.3 m/s against the 5.5 m/s cap. The simulated liftoff mass of 0.183 kg explains the overshoot; my airframe estimate of 0.25 kg was 36% heavy, and the thin air at 762 m does the rest.
5. Fix: apogee 676.8 m needs to come down to about 488 m, a ratio of 677 / 488 = 1.39. In the drag-dominated regime apogee scales roughly with mass, so I add about 0.07 kg of realistic payload: an altimeter and chute-release bay near the top of the body tube. New liftoff should be near 0.183 + 0.07 = 0.253 kg, which puts apogee close to 490 m. It also moves the CG forward, so the margin can only grow. Nothing else changes.

messages.reasoning_content:
4. Check: the simulated apogee of 657.4 m is still 35% over the 488 m goal, so the altitude target keeps failing; the extra 0.07 kg only bought 676.8 - 657.4 = 19.4 m, which says this rocket is speed-limited, not mass-limited, at 0.52 Mach. A new problem also shows up: the chute deploys at 8.1 s while apogee is at 8.67 s, so it opened at 24.5 m/s and the simulator flagged a high-speed deployment warning. Gates otherwise pass: rail exit 28.7 m/s, margin 3.15 cal, touchdown 4.9 m/s.
5. Fix: two changes aimed at the two causes. One, the altitude overshoot needs drag, not mass: body diameter 41.6 mm to 50 mm raises frontal area by (50 / 41.6)^2 = 1.45, and the thicker-walled tube adds about 0.03 kg of its own mass. Two, deployment speed 24.5 m/s comes from the chute firing 0.6 s before apogee: delay 6 s to 8 s puts the ejection charge about 1.5 s past apogee so the rocket opens while falling slowly. Fins scaled up a little to match the fatter tube. Re-simulating.

4. Check: simulated apogee is 567.5 m, still 16% above the 488 m goal and outside the 5% band. The deployment fix worked cleanly: the chute opened at 10.1 s, past the 9.9 s apogee, at only 2.7 m/s. Gates pass: rail exit 25.8 m/s, thrust-to-weight 11.4, margin 2.43 cal. But touchdown is now 5.4 m/s against the 5.5 m/s cap, which leaves almost no room to add mass.
5. Fix: apogee 567.5 m needs another cut of about 14%, and mass is nearly exhausted as a lever since landing is already at 5.4 m/s. The remaining lever is the motor itself: 56.7 N*s on this airframe overshoots, so I want a weaker motor in the same diameter class. Checking three candidates before re-simulating: E30T, F24W and F42T.

5. Fix: the F24W gives 47.3 N*s against the F32T's 56.7, a ratio of 47.3 / 56.7 = 0.83, close to the 488 / 567.5 = 0.86 apogee ratio I need. It is the same 24 mm diameter, so the mount is unchanged, and at 24.0 N average the thrust-to-weight on about 0.30 kg stays near 24 / (0.30 * 9.81) = 8.2 with rail exit near sqrt(2 * 69 * 1.83) = 15.9 m/s. The E30T at 33.7 N*s would cut too deep and probably undershoot, and F42T/L at 55.9 N*s changes nothing. Apogee on a slightly weaker motor peaks a touch later, so the delay goes from 8 s to the F24W's 7 s option. One motor swap, nothing else touched.

4. Check: simulated apogee is 480.7 m, 1.5% under the 488 m goal and finally inside the 5% band. Rail exit 22.0 m/s, thrust-to-weight 8.1, margin 2.33 cal, deployment at 9.1 s just before the 9.28 s apogee at 3.4 m/s. One number sits right on the limit: touchdown is 5.5 m/s against the 18 ft/s = 5.5 m/s cap, so it may be legal by a whisker or just over; that is not margin I want to fly with.
5. Fix: touchdown 5.5 m/s vs the 5.5 m/s limit. A 0.65 m chute (area 0.332 m^2) on the same 0.28 kg descent mass gives v = sqrt(2 * 0.28 * 9.81 / (1.1 * 0.8 * 0.332)) = 4.3 m/s at site density. That is the only change; the rocket, motor and payload stay as they are.

4. Check: simulated apogee is 474.4 m, 2.8% under the 488 m goal and inside the 5% band. Touchdown is 4.9 m/s, clear of the 5.5 m/s cap. Rail exit 21.5 m/s, thrust-to-weight 7.9, stability 2.4 cal at rail exit and through the burn, total impulse 47.3 N*s under the 160 N*s cap, chute out at 9.1 s just ahead of the 9.26 s apogee at 3.5 m/s. Every gate and every stated requirement passes.
5. Fix: none needed after the chute enlargement; this run passed everything.
6. Uncertainty: the whole result leans on OpenRocket's drag model at 762 m elevation and on the build mass matching 0.311 kg; a lighter real build flies higher and lands faster. Descent assumes the chute Cd 0.8 model value and packs a 0.65 m canopy into a 47 mm bay, which is snug. Wind was never stated, so 2 m/s was assumed; real wind moves the 171 m drift number around.
